doc_title: Introduction to Programming Languages and Compilers
topic: Introduction to Programming Languages and Compilers
key_facts: Programming languages are notations for describing computations to people and to machines.

Programming domains mentioned in this material include Scientific Applications (Fortran, ALGOL 60, Julia, MATLAB), Business Applications (COBOL, DATABUS, PL/B), Artificial Intelligence (LISP, Prolog), Systems Programming (PL/S, BLISS, C), and Web Software (XHTML, JavaScript, PHP, Java, C#).
Language evaluation criteria include: clarity/simplicity/unity, orthogonality, support of abstraction (control and data), and safety.
Orthogonality in language design means every combination of features is meaningful, and independent functions should be controlled by independent mechanisms.
The document is authored by Dr. Nguyen Hua Phung and MEng. Tran Ngoc Bao Duy from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, Ho Chi Minh University of Technology, VNU-HCM.
generated_text: Introduction to Programming Languages and Compilers Welcome! In this lesson, we will begin our journey into the world of programming languages. We'll explore what they are, the different domains they are used in, the compromises involved in their design, and how a computer actually understands and runs the code we write. What are Programming Languages? Programming languages are notations for describing computations to people and to machines. Different languages are designed for different purposes. Here are some common programming domains and examples of languages used in them: Scientific Applications: Fortran, ALGOL 60, Julia, MATLAB Business Applications: COBOL, DATABUS, PL/B Artificial Intelligence: LISP, Prolog Systems Programming: PL/S, BLISS, Extended ALGOL, C Web Software: XHTML, JavaScript, PHP, Java, C# (ASP.NET) Language Design Trade-Offs Creating a programming language involves balancing competing goals. There is no single "best" language, only languages that are better suited for certain tasks. This is due to design trade-offs: Reliability vs. cost of execution: For example, Java demands that all references to array elements be checked for proper indexing. This increases reliability but also leads to increased execution costs. Readability vs. writability: For example, APL provides many powerful operators, allowing complex computations to be written in a very compact program. However, this comes at the cost of poor readability. Writability (flexibility) vs. reliability: For example, C++ pointers are powerful and very flexible, but they are not always used reliably, which can lead to errors. Language Implementation: From Code to Execution Before a program can be run, it must first be translated into a form that a computer can execute. The software systems that perform this translation are called translators . There are several methods for implementing a programming language: Compilation: Programs are entirely translated into machine language and then executed. Pure Interpretation: Programs are translated and executed line-by-line. Hybrid Implementation Systems: A compromise between compilers and pure interpreters. Just-in-time Compiler: A compiler inside an interpreter that compiles frequently used methods ("hot methods"). Compilers A compiler translates a program from a source language to a target language all at once. A compiler is a program that can read a program in one language - the source language - and translate it into an equivalent program in another language - the target language. If the target program is an executable machine-language program, it can then be called by the user to process inputs and produce outputs. Pure Interpreters An interpreter, on the other hand, processes the program one statement at a time. A pure interpreter is another common kind of language processor. Instead of producing a target program as a translation, an interpreter appears to directly execute the operations specified in the source program on inputs supplied by the user. Summary In this lesson, we've learned that programming languages are notations for describing computations. They are used in various domains and their design involves critical trade-offs, such as balancing reliability with cost. Finally, we saw that for a computer to run a program, the code must be processed by a translator, which can be a compiler (translating the entire program at once) or an interpreter (executing the program line-by-line).
